We introduce BILBY-PRO, a systematically derived benchmark of structurally conserved functional motifs from PROSITE-linked experimental structures, comprising 220 cases from 174 PROSITE motif-pattern entries. Evaluating six recent scaffold-generation models reveals distinct patterns in target coverage and unique-solution yield: RFDiffusion and Proteina solve more targets, whereas ESM3 produces more unique successful scaffolds on the targets it solves. We further introduce BILBY-MD, a reference-based all-atom molecular dynamics evaluation framework. Applied to statically solved designs from the original MotifBench benchmark, it compares motif drift, scaffold drift, motif-contact preservation, and motif-dihedral free-energy landscapes against reference simulations. Of 55 statically solved model-problem pairs, 31 satisfy our MD-supported criterion and only 8 pass all checks. Compact, self-contained motifs are often MD-supported, whereas interface-like or context-dependent motifs fail more frequently. Static refolding success therefore provides useful evidence of local motif recovery but does not establish dynamical fidelity of the full scaffold. BILBY highlights three complementary axes of motif-scaffolding evaluation: target coverage, unique-solution yield, and MD-supported dynamical fidelity.
comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations & Datasets Track). 23 pages, 10 figures, including supplementary material. The first three authors contributed equally. BILBY-PRO dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/HFMI-PROFOUND/BILBY-PRO ; BILBY-MD code: https://github.com/PROFOUND-HFMI/BILBY-MD

paper_title: Towards Generalist Graph-Level Anomaly Detection
paper_abstract: Graph-level anomaly detection (GLAD) aims to identify graphs that deviate significantly from the majority. While recent advances have achieved competitive performance, existing approaches mainly follow a dataset-specific paradigm, requiring substantial in-domain data and training cost when applied to new application scenarios. This limits their scalability and practicality in real-world applications where labeled data is scarce and diverse domains are continuously emerging. In this paper, we investigate the problem of generalist GLAD, which seeks to learn a single unified model capable of detecting anomalous graphs across multiple domains with minimal supervision on the target data. This problem introduces key challenges, including learning transferable patterns from heterogeneous graph datasets and effective adaptation under limited supervision. To address these challenges, we propose GenGLAD, a generalist GLAD approach that leverages discriminative subgraph extraction as the core mechanism to learn transferable anomaly knowledge and enable efficient adaptation to new domains. Specifically, GenGLAD employs a graph neural network-based discriminative subgraph extraction model to learn the anomaly-discriminative substructures that distinguish anomalous and normal graphs across diverse domains. During the test-time adaptation phase, multi-dimensional discrepancies between the extracted subgraph and multi-level contextual information are calculated to characterize anomalies from multiple perspectives. For efficient adaptation, a lightweight scoring module is introduced to automatically decide the most informative signals, improving robustness against misleading patterns. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves strong performance, superior generalization ability, and improved data efficiency compared to existing methods.
comments: Accepted by NIPS26

paper_title: FlyingDrones: A Dataset and Benchmark for Optical Flow Estimation from UAV motion
paper_abstract: Optical flow is an important cue for drone analysis in aerial surveillance, airspace monitoring, and long-range target tracking, where motion remains informative when appearance is weak. Estimating the motion of small Unmanned Aerial Vehicles, however, is difficult because distant targets occupy few pixels, have low contrast, and move against complex dynamic backgrounds. Standard optical-flow benchmarks emphasize large, object-centric motions and therefore do not characterize distant aerial targets well. We introduce FlyingDrones, a generated benchmark with dense ground-truth optical flow and segmentation masks derived from physically based rendering, and define resolution-normalized metrics (EPE Norm) that normalize flow by image dimensions. We evaluate 16 state-of-the-art model families on a motion- and size-stratified subset of 999 flow pairs at three resolutions. Every family recovers drone motion better than the zero-flow reference, but the gap between families widens with resolution: at 1920x1080, global-matching, recurrent, transformer, and short-window temporal models separate clearly from pyramid, classical, self-supervised, lightweight, and diffusion models. Within-family checkpoint spread is comparable to or larger than between-family spread, so the training curriculum is as important as the architecture. Two complementary studies test the benchmark beyond synthetic accuracy: a ground-truth-free motion-alignment evaluation on 21 cameras of real UAV footage shows that the synthetic ranking carries a moderate, significant signal about real-world performance (Spearman \r{ho} = 0.63 over 41 checkpoints) while the exact top ranks differ, and a fine-tuning study shows that 800 FlyingDrones pairs reduce held-out drone-region error by up to 37% and improve drone localization on the real footage for all four architectures tested.
comments: NeurIPS 2026, https://neurips.cc/virtual/2026/loc/sydney/poster/138996

paper_title: MCPHallu: Benchmarking Reasoning, Execution, and Memory Hallucinations in MCP Agents
paper_abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which allows them to discover and invoke tools across multiple servers at runtime. Existing MCP benchmarks primarily measure task completion; where they diagnose failures, they do so after execution rather than building specific reasoning, execution, and memory failure risks into task construction.   We introduce MCPHallu, a benchmark for diagnosing hallucination-prone agent failures in MCP environments along three axes: reasoning, execution, and memory. MCPHallu contains 358 tasks across five capability domains and runs on 36 production MCP servers in isolated containers. Each task is designed with a structural trigger that makes one of four subtypes the dominant failure risk: Branch Collapse, Unreachable Goal, Tool Misuse, or Context Forgetting. This design enables subtype-level analysis rather than aggregate task success alone.   We evaluate fourteen frontier LLM agents from eight vendors on 5{,}012 trajectories. Current MCP agents remain vulnerable to hallucination-inducing tool environments, achieving an average score of 0.642 on a $[0,1]$ scale (higher is better). Failures concentrate on Unreachable Goal tasks, where the average score drops to 0.458 and 23.2\% of runs pass, indicating that agents often continue issuing tool calls or claim successful completion rather than recognizing infeasible goals. Subtype rankings diverge sharply: a model's rank shifts by 6.9 of 13 positions on average across subtypes, and Branch Collapse is uncorrelated with Unreachable Goal across models ($r = -0.12$). MCPHallu is released at https://github.com/J1zz/mcp_hallu.

paper_title: Beyond Instruction Override: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injection with Task-Tampering Attacks
paper_abstract: Indirect prompt-injection (IPI) benchmarks predominantly test planted instructions that redirect a tool-using agent toward an attacker-chosen task. Yet attacker-controlled content can instead tamper with the outcome of the task already in progress. A buyer's dispute evidence can cite a false refund policy to inflate a refund without changing the task. We define IPI by authority rather than instruction-like wording: planted content constitutes an attack when it attempts to influence a decision that its source is not authorized to determine. We introduce a benchmark that makes this boundary explicit: in each of 90 validated cases across three tool-use environments, the user request specifies the source that resolves the targeted decision. Every attack tampers with a decision required by the benign task rather than replacing that task. Each case has attacks with the same harmful outcome that target up to six parts of the agent's decision making: its objective, decision rules, available actions, expected consequences, reading of observations, or beliefs about the current state. Without a defense, attacks on three of the five other targets (decision rules, available actions, and state) have higher mean success than objective attacks across five LLMs. A detection-and-removal defense reduces objective-targeting attacks to 2.4% success but leaves observation- and state-targeting attacks at 9.5% and 12.1%; this gap persists under detection-optimized rewrites. A tool-policy defense still allows 15.4% attack success, close to 17.0% without a defense, because these attacks generally retain expected tools and manipulate values obtained during execution. Evaluations whose attacks redirect the task or target only the agent's objective can therefore overestimate the coverage of these defenses. Code and data are available at https://github.com/amazon-science/task-tampering-prompt-injection.
comments: 34 pages, 6 figures. Code and data: https://github.com/amazon-science/task-tampering-prompt-injection

paper_title: CST-Bench: Benchmarking Counterfactual Spatial Transition Reasoning with Causal Transition On-Policy Self-Distillation
paper_abstract: Spatial reasoning is a fundamental capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), yet existing benchmarks mainly focus on static scene understanding. When objects are moved or swapped, models must infer not only spatial relations but also how interventions change the scene state. To address this problem, we introduce CST-Bench, a benchmark for counterfactual spatial reasoning. CST-Bench contains 7,082 examples covering 6 intervention types and 12 transformation operators, with dense causal annotations including intervention sources, affected relations, expected effects, invariant relations, and metric changes. We benchmark general-purpose MLLMs on CST-Bench and further compare post-training strategies on CST-Bench and standard spatial benchmarks. Results show that methods effective for ordinary spatial reasoning can still fail under counterfactual interventions. We further formulate counterfactual spatial reasoning as causal state-transition modeling and propose CT-OPSD, which uses CST-Bench annotations to guide a teacher model in learning counterfactual state transitions and causal reasoning chains. These chains are then distilled into a student model that reasons only from real observations. Overall, experiment results establish CST-Bench as a challenging benchmark and reusable supervision resource for counterfactual spatial reasoning. CT-OPSD further provides an initial demonstration of how its annotations can support model improvement.
comments: 18 pages, 5 figures, 8 tables; includes technical supplementary material

paper_title: OPRD-Imp: a dataset of experimentally observed impurities and side products in multi-step pharmaceutical syntheses
paper_abstract: Predicting reaction impurities is a critical yet persistently data-limited challenge in pharmaceutical process chemistry. While machine learning models for reaction outcome prediction have advanced rapidly, benchmarking their ability to predict impurities remains impractical due to the absence of curated, publicly accessible datasets. We present OPRD-Imp, a dataset of 229 organic reactions drawn from 62 publications in Organic Process Research & Development, each annotated with experimentally observed impurities and their mechanistic origins. A total of 784 impurity entries is provided, classified into four origin categories. Reactions are represented as reaction SMILES and impurities as individual SMILES strings, with multi-step synthetic route connectivity preserved. All data were manually extracted from the source publications by trained chemists following a standardized extraction protocol, with expert chemical validation and manual structure drawing. OPRD-Imp is intended to serve as a benchmark resource for evaluating models that predict reaction impurities, providing experimentally reported impurity annotations and mechanistic origin labels that are not systematically represented in conventional reaction datasets.
comments: 15 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Dataset available at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.34075524

paper_title: Reweighting is not Harmless: Understanding the Role of Dataset Characteristics
paper_abstract: Reweighting is a widely used pre-processing method for promoting discrimination-free model behavior by assigning different weights to data points during model training. While it is often credited with improving fairness, particularly by mitigating systematic underestimation for underrepresented groups, it can also introduce unintended harms under certain data conditions. Using controlled simulations that vary group size and baseline event prevalence, we show how reweighting can yield misleading improvements in fairness by reducing underestimation for one group while introducing it for another. Across 3,000 simulated datasets with event prevalence of 7-14%, reweighting improved parity in positive classification and false negative rates (FNR) between groups, but did so partly by decreasing positive classifications and increasing FNR for the group with higher baseline prevalence. These effects were most pronounced when that group was a minority: its FNR rose by 6 percentage points, approximately 82 additional missed cases per 10,000 group members, and roughly three-quarters of the improvement in FNR parity came from this increase rather than from gains for the other group. The pattern held across six classifiers, from logistic regression to neural networks, while overall accuracy was essentially unchanged, leaving the shift invisible in aggregate performance metrics. These findings mirror patterns reported in real-world applications and underscore the critical role of data characteristics in shaping the impact of this fairness intervention. While reweighting may create desirable outcomes in some applications, practitioners should critically evaluate it relative to their problem area and goals. Specifically, when the goal is to reduce underestimation in one group without introducing underestimation in another, reweighting may not be the appropriate approach.

paper_title: MotionBench-XAI: Benchmarking What Shapes Shapley Explanations in Spatiotemporal Machine Learning
paper_abstract: Predicting outcomes from spatiotemporal data, such as assessing Parkinson's severity from human motion, often requires explainability in addition to accuracy. Practitioners need to know what drove the prediction, whether it be spatial (a body joint), temporal (a specific window), or both. Shapley values are attributions computed by treating input features as players in a cooperative game and measuring how the model output changes as coalitions of players are removed. Computing them involves choosing what counts as players, how absent players are imputed, and how the game is evaluated. How these choices affect explanation quality is poorly understood for spatiotemporal data, and real data carries no ground-truth attributions to check against. We present MotionBench-XAI, a benchmark built on i) five synthetic spatiotemporal datasets with exact ground-truth Shapley values, ii) three real datasets across clinical gait, electrocardiogram, and audio, iii) ten attribution methods across three player sets, and iv) three trained architectures. We show that grouping features into players, across time, space, or both, matters more than the choice of imputer. Generative imputers improve explanations only when their conditional models are accurate. On real data, the standard proxy metrics select contradictory best methods. We distill these findings into practical insights and provide an open-source pipeline.

paper_title: Not All Latents Are Equal: Importance-Weighted Latent Graph Generation
paper_abstract: Graph generation has shown tremendous effectiveness in modeling complex scientific tasks ranging from molecule generation to optimized circuit design. Most recent advancements have developed models that learn to denoise noisy graphs using either discrete diffusion or flow matching. However, discrete graph diffusion scales quadratically with the number of nodes, making it difficult to use such models on larger graphs. On the other hand, latent graph generation instead seeks to denoise noisy graph latents, which scale better to more nodes due to their lower dimension. However, in practice, latent graph generation models lag behind their discrete counterparts in performance. We study this problem, finding that it is caused by the unequal distribution of that different latent dimensions have on graph reconstruction. the impact. We observe that the vast majority of impact is contained in only a smaller number of latent dimensions. Since equal emphasis is placed on reconstructing the entire latent in the loss function, existing models are optimized to reconstruct information irrelevant to the downstream task. To tackle this problem, we propose Latent Importance Reweighting ({\bf LIR)} which weights each latent dimensions via it's importance to final graph reconstruction. Importance is calculated as the relative influence of a single latent unit on graph reconstruction, which is represented via the Jacobian of the decoder relative to the latent. Our method is model-agnostic and requires no additional model parameters or hyperparameters. Experiments show that LIR can boost performance and lead to faster training convergence when applied to two different autoencoders on various benchmark datasets. Code: https://github.com/biraaj/GraphGenLatentReweight

paper_title: Turkish Multimodal Video Fact-Checking: A New Dataset and a Comparison of Zero-Shot Agentic and Fine-Tuned Systems
paper_abstract: Video-based misinformation spreads rapidly on social media, but almost all existing fact-checking systems focus exclusively on English text. Tools for low-resource languages such as Turkish are severely limited. In this work, we present TeViD (Turkish Video Fact-checking Dataset), to the best of our knowledge the first multimodal video fact-checking dataset for Turkish. We compiled the dataset from articles published by Teyit.org, an IFCN-certified organisation, and enriched it with translated Snopes articles and synthetic examples to reduce class imbalance. Building on TeViD, we develop two verification pipelines that share the same open-source base model. First, in 3MFact-TR (Pipeline 1), we adapt the multi-role 3MFact framework to Turkish with the Qwen2.5-7B large language model and the Qwen2-VL-7B vision-language model, and add three modules of our own: a semantic inconsistency checker, a 5W1H question manager, and a bilingual evidence retriever that excludes fact-checking sites to prevent leakage. Second, as our Fine-Tuned Model (Pipeline 2), we fine-tune a single Qwen2.5-7B with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to produce closed-book verdicts from the claim and the video's textual description. We report accuracy, macro F1, True class F1, and True class recall for both systems, together with ablation studies.
comments: 11 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. MSc dissertation, Queen Mary University of London, 2026

paper_title: From Geometry to Function: A Multi-Task LiDAR Benchmark Dataset for Semantic and Functional Parsing of Urban Facades
paper_abstract: Understanding building facades is central to urban digital twins, heritage modelling, and sustainable city analysis, yet existing LiDAR benchmarks stop at geometry and semantic segmentation and offer little support for reasoning about the functional role of each architectural element. We introduce HFX3D, a large-scale urban facade benchmark of approximately 492 million LiDAR points from 26 buildings in Halifax, Canada, captured across four seasons, day and night, and varied weather. Each facade is annotated at three tiers, semantic, instance, and per-instance functional attributes, making it, to our knowledge, the first facade dataset to pair geometry and semantics with functional labels. Annotations are produced by a semi-automatic pipeline that combines geometry-guided heuristics with expert validation. We benchmark representative point-based, graph-based, convolutional, and transformer architectures and find that semantic segmentation is already challenging under severe class imbalance, while instance separation of repetitive structures and functional reasoning from geometry are substantially harder. The benchmark establishes a new foundation for function-aware 3D urban understanding. Project page: https://jijup.github.io/hfx3d-benchmark/ ; code: https://github.com/jijup/hfx3d-benchmark
comments: Accepted to WACV 2027. 19 pages (8 main + supplementary), includes appendix. Project page: https://jijup.github.io/hfx3d-benchmark/ ; Code: https://github.com/jijup/hfx3d-benchmark

paper_title: Benchmarking Machine Learning for Chaotic Three-Body Dynamics in Astrophysics
paper_abstract: Machine learning (ML) and generative AI have recently made impressive progress in understanding physics. We explore a hierarchy of prediction problems stemming from chaotic three-body systems and benchmark existing ML approaches, including general-purpose prediction algorithms and those that build on top of foundational physics models. We first simulate the trajectories of triple systems near the critical boundary of stable/unstable initial conditions. We then design a hierarchy of learning tasks, focusing mainly on two broad problems: stability prediction and trajectory prediction. The former classifies whether a given triple system has diverged or not up to a specific horizon, while the latter predicts the exact trajectory, both given suitable input features. We benchmark a range of ML approaches, from simple regression methods to state-of-the-art foundational physics models, across these tasks, and compare them against astrophysical methods such as the Mardling-Aarseth stability criterion. Our experiments reveal a clear order of task difficulties in chaotic three-body dynamics: early dynamics enable strong stability prediction, while precise long-horizon trajectory forecasting remains difficult. Code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/Simonwan03/ThreeBodyMLBench.
comments: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Sim2Science: ML with Imperfect Scientific Models

paper_title: Not All Misalignment Is Alike: A Decomposed Benchmark for Emergent Misalignment
paper_abstract: Emergent misalignment (EM), in which fine-tuning on a narrow task induces misaligned behaviour on unrelated prompts, has been demonstrated across a wide range of datasets, model families, and training setups. Yet, most studies continue to rely on the evaluation approach introduced in the original EM paper, producing rates that are sensitive to the small set of evaluation questions used, the choice of judge, and the thresholds applied. These evaluations can also conflate misalignment with capability loss and offer little insight into the specific ways misalignment manifests. Differences in datasets, models, and fine-tuning configurations further make findings difficult to compare across studies. We introduce EMERGE, a decomposed benchmark that tracks changes in eight distinct misaligned behaviours from base to fine-tuned models. It evaluates these behaviours on out-of-domain prompts against matched benign controls and tracks capability, coherence, and refusal to account for potential confounders. Applying EMERGE to 8 open-weight models and 13 fine-tuning datasets, we find that models with similar broad misalignment rates can exhibit very different behavioural profiles that a single score cannot capture. We hope EMERGE can help establish a shared and robust standard for measuring EM, making findings more comparable and helping move research from detecting the phenomenon towards understanding it.

paper_title: Towards Label-Efficient Geospatial Foundation Model Adaptation via Positive-Unlabeled Learning for Building Damage Mapping
paper_abstract: Geospatial foundation models (GFMs) are reshaping remote sensing by shifting the field from task-specific modeling toward general-purpose geospatial intelligence. Mapping the damage to buildings stands to benefit substantially from this shift, as GFMs pretrained on large-scale Earth observation data provide generalizable geospatial representations that can facilitate effective responses to sudden-onset disasters. Although parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) facilitates GFM adaptation, parameter efficiency does not necessarily translate into label efficiency. Building damage mapping remains challenging due to scarce pre-existing labeled data or limited time for annotation. When weak supervision is introduced to alleviate the labeling bottleneck, we identify the difficulty of learning sufficiently discriminative representations as a key challenge for label-efficient GFM adaptation. To address this challenge, we propose a Positive-Unlabeled GFM Adaptation (PUMA) framework that requires annotations for only a small number of damaged buildings. More specifically, PUMA integrates non-contrastive weakly supervised representation refinement to mitigate the impact of noisy supervision on representation learning from a gradient perspective, and latent-state-based label disambiguation to enable reversible supervision refinement without requiring class prior estimation. Extensive experiments on disaster benchmark datasets from around the world demonstrated the effectiveness and robustness of PUMA. A real-world application to the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires further highlighted its potential to accurately map damage under highly limited supervision. More broadly, these findings suggest that weakly supervised PEFT offers a label-efficient pathway from GFMs to real-world applications.

paper_title: ResidentBench: A Common-Sense and Situational Awareness Benchmark—How Do Language Models Act When Left to Their Own Judgment?
paper_abstract: As language models gain access to tools, they may encounter situations for which no task or instructions have been supplied. Performance on assigned tasks does not establish how they act in that condition. ResidentBench evaluates language models exposed to declarative sensors and actuators without an author-assigned task, goal, mission, purpose, role, persona or request to deliberate or act. A shared harness records tool calls and environmental trajectories; a separate evaluator receives the situation-specific context needed to judge those actions. The proof-of-concept study tests ten model configurations in five simulated scenarios: thermostat regulation, traffic control, fictional nuclear-launch restraint, paddle-screen interaction and a refunded parcel delivered later. Ten episodes per configuration and scenario yield 500 completed episodes and 24,000 unique decisions. Each completed episode receives a retrospective contextual judgment. The general scoring rule combines repeated binary judgments with equal scenario weights on a scale from 0 to 100. A fixed 20-scenario Standard 1.0 suite remains future work, and no full-suite score is reported here. However, one grim fact about the current experimental results is that, across one hundred nuclear episodes with ten matched descriptions per model, some configurations never activated the fictional control, others activated it in a subset of runs, and one activated it in all ten runs.
comments: Preprints.org

paper_title: Can Large Language Models Tune Fraud Detection Models? Evidence from Three Public Fraud Datasets
paper_abstract: Machine-learning fraud detectors have settings (hyperparameters) that must be tuned by trial and error. We tested whether large language models (LLMs) can do this tuning. In a pre-registered study, Claude Opus 5.5 proposed settings for two gradient-boosting models, XGBoost and LightGBM, on three public fraud benchmarks. We compared it with random search and a Bayesian optimiser (TPE), testing every model on a later period than it was tuned on, with 10 repeats per condition. After 10 trials, the LLM matched what TPE reached after 40 trials on two benchmarks (all differences under 0.011 PR-AUC, p ≥ 0.07), but not on the third (0.008–0.011 lower, p ≤ 0.003). A smaller model, Claude Haiku 5.5, did as well at about 3% of the cost. Naming the dataset in the prompt did not help. When the trial scores shown to the LLM were altered, its proposals followed the altered scores (79% of cases, p<0.001). Where the tuning data held only 28 frauds, tuning scores were negatively related to later performance. Contrary to common advice, tuning on the most recent data did not select better models than tuning on a random sample, because it stopped training too early.
comments: Preprints.org

paper_title: Data Descriptor: Multimodal Dataset of Bioreactor Cell Cultivations Including Turbidity, Permittivity, O<sub>2</sub> and CO<sub>2</sub> Measurements
paper_abstract: We present a comprehensive, time-resolved dataset of Chinese Hamster Ovary (CHO) cultivation dynamics to support data-driven bioprocess engineering and process analytical technology development. The dataset includes 24 controlled bioreactor cultivations, representing 12 experiments performed in duplicate in a parallel bioreactor system with a working volume of 0.55 – 0.8 L and cultivation durations of 161.5 – 328.5 h. A total of 48 variables are provided, comprising 38 continuous inline variables and 10 offline variables sampled up to twice daily. In addition to standard process measurements, the dataset includes multimodal inline monitoring using turbidity, permittivity, and dissolved CO2 sensors. The experiments systematically vary cultivation medium, agitation rate, aeration rate, and process mode (batch and fed-batch), providing diverse operating conditions for sensor evaluation, process modeling, and bioprocess analysis. Furthermore, the inoculation cell density, glutamine concentration, and impeller position were varied to further expand the range of investigated process conditions. The dataset preserves realistic measurement characteristics, including noise, and missing values, enabling robust benchmarking of data-driven methods for process monitoring, modeling, and control.
comments: Preprints.org

paper_title: Performance and Response Consistency of 52 Small Language Models in a Japanese Pharmacy Benchmark: A Comparative Study
paper_abstract: Objective: Small language models (SLMs) suitable for local deployment may enable integration of generative AI into electronic health record (EHR) systems; however, their performance in non-English pharmaceutical domains remains unclear. Methods: Fifty-two open-source SLMs (≤20B parameters) were evaluated using 283 text-based questions from the 107th Japanese National License Examination for Pharmacists. Each model was tested in three independent runs. Performance was assessed using accuracy and response consistency metrics, including the Any Correct Rate, Full Correct Rate, and Consistency Gap. Results: Three models (GPT-OSS:20b, Qwen3:14b, and Qwen3:8b) achieved high accuracy comparable to frontier LLMs, whereas medical-specialized SLMs performed poorly. Consistency Gap showed no association with parameter size but demonstrated a nonlinear relationship with accuracy. Conclusions: Selected locally deployable SLMs achieved strong performance in a Japanese pharmaceutical benchmark, supporting their potential as components of EHR-compatible decisionsupport systems, provided that their reliability is further validated in clinical contexts.
comments: Preprints.org

paper_title: When Does Grid-State-Aware Parameter Adaptation Help Metaheuristic Dispatch of Photovoltaic Distributed Generation? A Reproducible Multi-Feeder Benchmark
paper_abstract: Metaheuristic optimisation is widely used for distribution-network operation, yet claims of superiority are often based on single cases without equal budgets, deterministic references, or reproducible seeds. This study evaluates a fuzzy-adaptive particle swarm optimiser using voltage-deviation and renewable-ramp inputs (FA-PSO-UR) for the dispatch of inverter-interfaced photovoltaic (PV) distributed generation (DG). It is compared with a genetic algorithm (GA), classical particle swarm optimisation (PSO), differential evolution (DE), a grey wolf optimiser (GWO), and time-varying PSO (TV-PSO) on the IEEE 33- and 69-bus feeders. The frozen benchmark comprises 1,080 static runs and 720 sequential 24-hour runs under smooth and cloud-driven PV profiles, with paired seeds and identical function-evaluation budgets. DE achieves the lowest static median in all six cases, whereas FA-PSO-UR is engineering-equivalent to PSO in all six and to TV-PSO in five. All sequential schedules are feasible. FA-PSO-UR achieves the lowest median objective in three of four sequential scenarios, with median gaps of 0.0056–0.0212% to the best-known deterministic references. TV-PSO ranks first for the IEEE 69-bus smooth profile, where the two methods remain engineering-equivalent. FA-PSO-UR shows practical superiority only over selected weaker baselines, not over PSO or TV-PSO. Physical-state-aware adaptation therefore provides selective dynamic benefit rather than universal dominance.
comments: Preprints.org

paper_title: Rug Pulls in the IoT and DePIN Ecosystem: Patterns, Red Flags, and Risk Mitigation
paper_abstract: Rug pulls remain one of the most pervasive and damaging forms of fraud in blockchain-based ecosystems. While a growing body of research has examined these schemes in conventional decentralized finance settings, far less attention has been paid to the distinctive risks that arise when token incentives are combined with physical infrastructure. Decentralized Physical Infrastructure Networks (DePIN) and related Internet of Things (IoT) projects often require participants to invest in hardware while relying on token rewards, creating hybrid risk surfaces that differ from purely digital token environments. This paper presents a structured, literature-based analysis of rug pulls in the IoT and DePIN ecosystem. Drawing on existing studies of smart-contract vulnerabilities, liquidity manipulation, serial scammer behavior, and detection methods, we develop a taxonomy of rug-pull patterns that incorporates both classic mechanisms and those linked to hardware sales, controllable emissions, and operational abandonment. We consolidate practical red flags across contract, liquidity, hardware-incentive, and operational dimensions, and introduce simple quantitative indicators to support more consistent risk assessment. Building on these elements, we propose a multi-layered mitigation framework organized around prevention, monitoring, and response. The contribution is deliberately conceptual. Rather than introducing new datasets or detection models, the paper synthesizes scattered insights into a coherent analytical structure tailored to the hybrid nature of IoT and DePIN projects. In doing so, it highlights critical gaps in current research and offers a practical foundation for participants, evaluators, and future empirical studies seeking to reduce exposure to exit scams at the intersection of blockchain incentives and physical infrastructure.
comments: Preprints.org

paper_title: Spacetime: A Library for Cleaning and Combining Disparate Spatiotemporal Datasets in Python
paper_abstract: As climate change accelerates, spatiotemporal climate and weather data rasters are increasingly used in academic research, agriculture, infrastructure, and other disci-plines across public and private domains. Unfortunately, these raster data are often stored under numerous file types with different spatial and temporal boundaries, spa-tial reference systems, and spatial and temporal resolutions. The tools and workflows that we have are often hindered by coordinate reference system mismatches, data type mismatches, data aggregation mismatches, and other fundamental challenges. To fully harness the impacts of these data, software tools are needed that can be leveraged effi-ciently and intuitively and without a steep learning curve for the new user. In this pa-per, we introduce Spacetime, a novel programming library in Python that enables effi-cient spatiotemporal data processing, management, alignment, and analysis. Spacetime is an open-source project written in Python that provides a set of powerful functions to manipulate spatiotemporal data in a single, unified library. Spacetime’s overarching themes are simplicity and usability. However, the library does not com-promise processing speed. In our comparison, it was as fast or faster than other popu-lar Python libraries, while requiring many fewer lines of code and no external loops or control functions. We hope this library will lower the barrier of entry to scientists in fields that have not traditionally used spatiotemporal raster data but are doing so in-creasingly frequently in the current climate.
comments: Preprints.org

paper_title: Beyond Benchmark Accuracy: A Hybrid Framework for Phishing URL and Email Detection
paper_abstract: Phishing detectors can achieve almost perfect accuracy on benchmark datasets and still struggle with the links people encounter in practice. This paper investigates that gap and describes a hybrid framework for assessing URLs and emails through machine learning, language analysis, header inspection, and transparent rules. Our URL model combines character-level TF-IDF with 17 lexical features in a logistic regression classifier. Analysis of the 235,795 URLs in PhiUSIIL revealed pronounced differences in how the two classes were represented: every legitimate example used a simple HTTPS domain format, while 59.9% of phishing URLs included a path and 51.3% used HTTP. A classifier trained on raw URLs achieved 99.71% test accuracy, yet incorrectly marked 26 of 30 ordinary legitimate links as phishing. To limit reliance on these patterns, we trained a second classifier on 197,591 unique registered domains. On held-out domains, it achieved 86.02% accuracy, a ROC-AUC of 0.892, and 89.02% phishing precision. We then combined its predictions with URL-pattern checks, NLTK-based email cues, and SPF, DKIM, and DMARC evidence in a Flask prototype that reports a risk score and supporting reasons. The results show why dataset composition and realistic tests matter as much as headline accuracy when evaluating phishing detection.
comments: Preprints.org

paper_title: Origami as a Spatial and Geometric Reasoning Benchmark
paper_abstract: Multimodal language models perform well on visual recognition and on tool use, but these abilities do not transfer directly to spatial and geometric reasoning. Geometric structure does not reduce to text or to a single image: exact angles and incidences, which surface lies in front of which, and the order in which operations were applied are not recoverable from a semantic description of a scene. We introduce CP2Seq, a benchmark for evaluating geometric reasoning and sequential planning in multimodal language models through origami. The benchmark contains 600 procedurally generated samples, each requiring a model to produce a valid sequence of folds from a crease pattern and a target folded state. Samples are produced by a deterministic folding engine. Ground truth is recorded during generation. We release the generation and evaluation framework to support additional samples and experiments across reference depths and action models. During evaluation, the engine executes proposed folds or rejects invalid actions with explicit feedback, while the model remains responsible for selecting actions and searching for a solution. We evaluate multimodal language models under progressively greater tool assistance, and against a deterministic breadth-first search over the same action set. Candidate sequences are assessed by executing them and comparing the resulting folded state with the target, allowing for planar translations, rotations, and reflections. Performance falls off sharply with sequence depth: in the Luna ablations no configuration solves a medium or hard sample (11 or more folds), while some-layers solves rise from 6/30 to 18/30 with higher reasoning effort. Failures are dominated by search rather than by illegal moves: in the broader evaluation, 48% of episodes end by revisiting earlier states. A breadth-first search over the same actions, under its own time budget, solves 54.7% of easy-group attempts, so short sequences are within reach of systematic search.
comments: Preprints.org

paper_title: BEAKER: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Embodied Brains in Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories
paper_abstract: Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories (SDCLs) are moving chemical experimentation toward embodied automation, where machines must perceive laboratory scenes, reason about experimental states, and act under physical, procedural, and safety constraints. Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly considered as embodied brains for such systems, existing laboratory benchmarks mainly focus on safety, anomaly detection, or general scientific understanding, leaving their execution-oriented embodied capabilities underexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce BEAKER, a Benchmark for evaluating Embodied Actionability, Knowledge, Experimentation, and Reasoning in SDCLs. BEAKER contains 1,000 expert-curated question-answer samples across 11 image and video task types, covering key judgments required for chemical laboratory execution, including affordance grounding, trajectory planning, equipment, state, and safety recognition, apparatus setup, operation and step reasoning, and temporal procedure reasoning. All questions and annotations are manually created and reviewed by chemistry and embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI) experts, without AI-assisted generation or annotation. We evaluate 28 general-purpose, science-oriented, chemistry-specialized, and embodied MLLMs in an offline, single-turn setting. Results show that current models can follow coarse experimental procedures in videos, but still struggle to ground actions into operable regions and feasible trajectories, to recognize fine-grained laboratory apparatus, states, and safety norms, and to order steps in mid-length procedures. BEAKER thus reveals a clear gap between coarse procedural understanding and the precise, action-grounded perception required for laboratory execution, providing a diagnostic benchmark for future MLLMs in SDCLs.
comments: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026 (Track on Evaluations and Datasets, Spotlight)

paper_title: LongBanana: An Expert-Verified Benchmark for Long-Context Multi-Reference Image Synthesis
paper_abstract: We introduce LongBanana, to our knowledge the first expert-designed and expert-verified benchmark for long-context multi-reference image synthesis in the age of agent-driven image generation. The task requires retrieving dispersed visual evidence, rejecting distractors, binding entities and relations, and composing one coherent final image from multiple references. LongBanana contains 90 carefully designed tasks organized by a 3-by-3 taxonomy; each task includes about 32 reference images, 20 constraints, and 50 evaluation items, yielding 4,670 expert-specified atomic evaluation items in total. Its graph-grounded evaluation design instantiates each task with reference images and an entity-relation graph, then converts node, edge, and whole-graph obligations into checklist items for Content Fidelity, Relational Binding, and Global Constraint Satisfaction. Reviewed expert labels include a 15% double-labeled subset with 89.4% exact agreement and 0.83 quadratic weighted kappa. We further introduce LongBanana-Gen, an agent-harness framework for long-horizon image generation; experiments show that minimal agent harnesses improve over direct generation, while a ReAct-Plan-Exec-Reflect (RPR) workflow yields harness-dependent gains by strengthening evidence grounding and repair. Together, LongBanana provides an auditable testbed for measuring dense visual evidence use and a shared target for developing stronger agent-driven image-generation systems. Code and data are available at the project page: https://long-banana.com/.
comments: NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations and Datasets Track. Project page: https://long-banana.com/

paper_title: Benchmarking Fine-Grained Visual Reasoning for Remote Sensing in Urban Management
paper_abstract: Fine-grained visual reasoning is essential for remote sensing in urban management, yet remains underexplored in the evaluation of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). We introduce UMBench, a fine-grained urban remote sensing benchmark built from unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) images for multiple urban management tasks such as traffic monitoring, urban construction, environmental quality, and disaster warning. Evaluations on UMBench reveal that current MLLMs often rely on scene-level priors and overlook fine-grained visual evidence. To address this issue, we further propose a novel evidence-first chain-of-thought method that directs models to inspect fine-grained visual evidence in a training-free manner. Experiments show that our method can improve the performance of both open-source and commercial MLLMs on UMBench.
comments: Accepted by IEEE AP-GARSS 2026; 4 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables

paper_title: Human Motion Prediction via Continual Prior Compensation
paper_abstract: Human Motion Prediction (HMP) aims to predict future human poses at different moments according to observed past motion sequences. Previous approaches mainly treated the prediction of different temporal moments as a single prediction task and learned the predictions of varied moments simultaneously, which would encounter a main limitation: the learning of short-term predictions (referring to ``near-future'' prediction) could be hindered by the predictions of long-term (referring to ``far-future'' prediction) motions. In this paper, we develop a novel temporal continual learning framework called Continual Prior Compensation (CPC) to progressively train HMP models, in which we divide the prediction task of motions corresponding to varied temporal moments into several subtasks and train the model in a multi-stage manner. To mitigate the prior information forgetting in the progressive training, we further introduce a learnable random variable Prior Compensation Factor (PCF) to explicitly measure the prior knowledge loss. We theoretically show that the PCF can be efficiently learned together with the model parameters by minimizing a reasonable upper bound of the objective function. The proposed CPC is further enhanced to estimate the prior information loss for each subtask and a new framework called Continual Prior Compensation++ (CPC++) with Fine-Grained Prior Compensation Factor (FGPCF) is finally developed. Our CPC and CPC++ frameworks are quite flexible and can be easily integrated with different HMP backbone models and adapted to various datasets and applications. Extensive experiments on three HMP benchmark datasets using multiple SOTA HMP backbones (PGBIG, siMLPe, MotionMixer, and LTD) demonstrate the effectiveness and flexibility of our frameworks.

paper_title: AmbiHTMLBench: A Benchmark for HTML-based Visually Rich Document parsing
paper_abstract: Traditional document parsing systems use Markdown as their output representation, which is effective for linear text but does not fully preserve fine-grained spatial structure, table geometry, visual hierarchy, or rendering semantics. We show that HTML is advantageous for heterogeneous and layout-sensitive documents whose representations must remain editable, inspectable, and reusable, and introduce AmbiHTMLBench to systematically study this setting. In this benchmark, given a real-world document, a model must recover executable HTML that preserves its content, organization, and visual appearance. The benchmark contains 1,115 diverse pages with structured annotations and evaluates predictions in two different ways: The objective protocol aligns ground-truth and predicted rendered blocks and measures table fidelity, page-level text error, and a two-dimensional layout consistency; a complementary reference-anchored protocol measures perceived fidelity by aligning LLM judges with human preferences. Across ten primary multimodal systems, the best objective score is 0.8092, while the subjective winner is different, demonstrating that automatic decomposition and human-perceived fidelity capture complementary properties. We further fine-tune a small-parameter expert model and find that task-specific adaptation yields good performance on document-to-HTML reconstruction task. These results position AmbiHTMLBench as a diagnostic testbed for building smarter and more logical document parsing systems.
comments: Check latest benchmark info on https://ambihtmlbench.tech

paper_title: Flexible Intensities Matter: A Comprehensive Re-evaluation of Hawkes Processes and Neural Temporal Point Processes
paper_abstract: Temporal point processes (TPPs) are the canonical framework for event sequence data, with applications spanning seismology, social media, and electronic health records. Recently, neural TPPs have been reported to substantially outperform classical TPPs, such as Hawkes processes, but these comparisons pitted flexible neural models against Hawkes processes in their most restricted form, and did not consider large-scale medical data. Here, we revisit this comparison through a systematic evaluation of Poisson and Hawkes processes of increasing flexibility against neural TPPs, on five established benchmark datasets and on two large-scale medical evaluation tasks derived from UK Biobank disease histories and MIMIC-IV ICU records, under autoregressive next-event prediction. First, the previously reported gap between Hawkes processes and neural TPPs largely disappears once Hawkes processes are equipped with flexible, learnable baselines and kernels. Second, the flexibility of the intensity parametrization also limits prior neural TPPs: a Transformer with a spline-based intensity head outperforms previous intensity-based neural TPPs and is on par with the intensity-free model. Decomposing the log-likelihood into a time term $\log p(t)$ and a type term $\log p(d \mid t)$, we find that this flexibility advantage lies almost entirely in the time density: more flexibility does not improve the type term. On these benchmarks, the gains of neural TPPs thus lie mostly in modeling when events occur, not which. Third, our results underscore the value of complex datasets for evaluating TPPs: only on the MIMIC-IV ICU records do neural TPPs retain an advantage in the type term. Our results inform both future method development and model choice. We release our framework, TorchPP, as an open-source package with consistent implementations of classical and neural TPPs.
comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 36 pages, 3 figures, 25 tables. Code: https://github.com/PMBio/torchPP (paper reproduction on branch neurips2026)

paper_title: A Systematic Benchmark for Evaluating Multimodal Personalized Reasoning of Vision-Language Models
paper_abstract: People often make decisions by holistically reasoning over heterogeneous forms of personal information. In this paper, we study the relatively underexplored capability of multimodal personalized reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). To this end, we introduce \texttt{MPRBench}, a novel and comprehensive benchmark specifically designed to evaluate personalized reasoning across a wide range of tasks and real-world challenges. \texttt{MPRBench} consists of 12 sub-tasks and additionally supports interpretable analysis of representative error cases. Through extensive experiments, we find that current personalized MLLMs still struggle with personalized reasoning due to several key challenges, including inaccurate recognition of personalized concepts and sensitivity to irrelevant personal information. We hope that MPRBench will stimulate further research on personalized reasoning in MLLMs. Code and data are available at https://github.com/kkdh15/MPRBench
comments: Accepted to WACV 2027

paper_title: DSRS: Teaching MLLMs to Perceive, Reason, and Segment in Complex Driving Scenes
paper_abstract: Existing reasoning segmentation frameworks typically employ multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with broad world knowledge to extract semantics in a human-like manner and generate corresponding segmentation masks. Nevertheless, these frameworks lack the necessary scene-specific awareness. This paper introduces driving scene reasoning segmentation (DSRS), a scene-specific task that requires models to interpret implicit instructions, infer spatial relations, detect potential risks, handle challenging conditions, and comprehend underlying traffic rules, ultimately generating accurate segmentation masks. Meanwhile, we establish a benchmark dataset to facilitate future research on the DSRS task. To pioneer this task, we propose DSRS-Net, a novel architecture with advanced reasoning segmentation capability for automated driving. Specifically, DSRS-Net seamlessly infuses geometric features for deeper reasoning segmentation, without compromising the original multimodal fusion mechanism. This strategy effectively mitigates the modality representation mismatch in MLLMs caused by RGB-only pretraining, while enhancing the integration of geometric, contextual, and linguistic features. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior performance of DSRS-Net in both driving scene reasoning segmentation and other language-driven segmentation tasks across various public datasets. The source code and dataset will be released upon publication.
comments: 26 pages and 19 figures

paper_title: Semantic Prior-Guided Incomplete Cross-Modal Retrieval with Noisy Labels
paper_abstract: Cross-modal retrieval (CMR) aims to bridge the semantic gaps between modalities by learning shared representations. Unfortunately, due to the dynamism and inconsistencies in real-world data acquisition, multimodal datasets frequently encounter severe modality incompleteness. Existing incomplete CMR methods adhere to a label-driven paradigm, relying heavily on categorical annotations as the semantic benchmark. However, label noise is difficult to avoid and often coexists with modality incompleteness. To address this challenge, we propose a novel semantic prior-guided framework for incomplete cross-modal retrieval with noisy labels, termed SPIRN. Specifically, SPIRN uses fixed semantic priors as a consistent reference for robust representation learning, noisy-label handling, and missing-modality completion. Based on this reference, Semantic Priors Guidance (SPG) establishes a stable category-level semantic space, Quality-aware Robust Learning (QRL) dynamically evaluates sample quality to distinguish clean samples from noisy ones and handles noise via reverse learning, Prior-guided Global Label Calibration (PGLC) rectifies corrupted annotations for refined supervision, and Confidence-driven Selective Imputation (CSI) recovers missing modalities from a cross-modal memory bank while filtering unreliable imputations with an increasing threshold. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first framework to jointly tackle the dual challenges of modality incompleteness and label noise in the CMR community. Extensive experiments on four widely used benchmark datasets demonstrate that SPIRN outperforms 11 state-of-the-art methods in various scenarios involving both missing modalities and noisy labels.

paper_title: Beyond Risk Cues: A Mechanism-Level Benchmark and Verifiable Debate for Scam Video Detection on the Web
paper_abstract: Online scam videos pose significant threats to individuals and society. Existing studies primarily focus on binary classification, offering limited insights into how scams work and the reasoning behind detection decisions. Moreover, they often overlook the challenge of distinguishing scam videos from superficially similar non-scam content, such as advertisements, and the robustness of detection models against misleading arguments. These limitations hinder reliable scam video detection. To address these limitations, we introduce MechScam, a benchmark comprising 6,614 videos covering diverse scam mechanisms and non-scam categories. MechScam provides explanations supported by video evidence, annotations of potential scam elements and their context, and misleading arguments constructed from genuine evidence. Recognizing that genuine evidence can still be used to justify misleading conclusions, we further propose ScamCourt, a debate framework in which trained prosecution and defense debaters present opposing arguments, while a trained judge makes decisions based on a transcript with verified citations. Extensive experiments show that state-of-the-art MLLMs struggle to distinguish scam videos from similar non-scam content. ScamCourt outperforms larger MLLMs and same-backbone fine-tuned baselines, reducing false positives and showing stronger resistance to misleading arguments. Together, MechScam and ScamCourt contribute to more reliable and interpretable scam video detection. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/SuperYFan/MechScam.

paper_title: GeoBiaset: A Counterfactual Benchmark for Demographic Bias in World-Level Geolocalization
paper_abstract: World-level image geolocalization is an increasingly important task, yet the biases of current models remain poorly understood. Prior work has identified coarse dataset imbalances noting, for instance, that some cities are absent from training sets and that models tend to perform better in wealthier regions. However, no one has yet examined which visual cues drive these disparities. To do so, we introduce GeoBiaset, the first benchmark designed to measure how geolocalization models are influenced by the apparent race of a person inserted into the image foreground. The dataset consists of 9,541 images, pairing existing geotagged background images with counterfactual edits spanning seven races, holding the ground-truth coordinates fixed. Controlled masking experiments show that occlusion and background drift do not fully explain geolocalization degradation. Alongside the benchmark, we introduce the Person-Origin Perturbation Indicators (POPI), novel metrics that quantify model resilience to these demographic perturbations by measuring whether predictions are pulled toward the region associated with the inserted group. Our evaluation of state-of-the-art geolocalization and multimodal large language models reveals a 16-47% drop in continent-level performance when a subject from a demographically mismatched group is inserted. A landmark versus no-landmark analysis and gradient-weighted heatmaps show that models preferentially attend to geographic landmarks when present, but shift attention to facial features in their absence.
comments: Accepted at Neurips 2026, E&D track. Project page: https://miccunifi.github.io/GeoBiaset/

paper_title: Catastrophic Overfitting is Weight Drift the Training Loss Cannot See
paper_abstract: Fast adversarial training (FAT) makes robust training affordable by replacing the multi-step attack with a single-step one, but it suffers from catastrophic overfitting (CO): partway through training, robustness to multi-step attacks collapses to near zero while the single-step attack used for training keeps being repelled. We show that CO is a quiet escape of the weights. Across the event the network's clean behavior quietly improves, and moving from the weights just before CO to those just after it changes the training objective only marginally while destroying most of the robustness. The training objective is therefore nearly blind to the displacement it causes, so it exerts no force to undo it. The exponential moving average (EMA) of the weights, which FAT protocols already maintain, does not accumulate this drift and stays robust through the entire event. This observation suggests a nearly free fix: when validation robustness drops, reset the weights to their EMA. We build this guard on top of a coupling-based base method designed so that its average stays inside the robust region. The resulting training removes CO in every one of our runs and attains the strongest AutoAttack accuracy among fast methods on all three benchmark datasets, including a clear margin on CIFAR-100, where it also clears the multi-step reference at roughly half its cost. Code is available at https://github.com/fzjcdt/co-weight-drift.
comments: 12 pages (including appendix), 7 figures, 6 tables. Code available at https://github.com/fzjcdt/co-weight-drift

paper_title: Alleviating Limited Effectiveness and Multi-Class Collapse in Deep Graph-level Clustering
paper_abstract: Given a collection of $N$ graphs, graph-level clustering (GLC) seeks to partition the $N$ graphs into semantically meaningful groups, which serves as a fundamental task in analyzing graph-structured data. While Graph Isomorphism Networks (GINs) have become the de facto encoders for GLC, they still fail to distinguish graphs due to their neglect of global topology. On top of that, existing deep clustering frameworks suffer from severe "clustering collapse" issues, particularly in imbalanced multi-class scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose S$^3$GLC, a novel framework that integrates global topological characteristics with local neighborhood features for balanced GLC. Theoretically, we leverage the Hoffman-Wielandt inequality to construct Spectral Signature as a rigorous lower bound for graph edit distance (GED), providing a computationally efficient proxy for global topological features. We additionally propose a joint manifold-preserving sparse regression module to fuse Spectral Signature with Spatial Representation, eliminating noise while preserving the complementary information. Furthermore, to mitigate clustering collapse, we introduce a balanced clustering objective based on optimal transport, harnessing the Sinkhorn-Knopp normalization to enforce equipartition constraints on cluster assignments. Extensive experiments on 10 real-world datasets demonstrate that S$^3$GLC significantly outperforms 15 state-of-the-art baselines, achieving remarkable improvements on benchmark datasets such as REDDIT-12K and OGBG-PPA.

paper_title: MotoVerse: A Benchmark for Predictive Perception of Motorized Two-Wheelers in Dense Unstructured Traffic
paper_abstract: Motorized Two-Wheelers (MTWs) dominate personal transport across much of the Global South, yet remain largely overlooked in predictive perception research for autonomous driving and ADAS. We introduce MotoVerse, a benchmark for predictive perception from an MTW's ego-centric perspective. MotoVerse comprises 949 maneuver clips collected in dense, unstructured traffic and trajectory annotations for over 31,000 surrounding road agents, including over 16,000 MTWs, enabling two complementary tasks: Ego-Rider Maneuver Anticipation (ERMA) and Traffic Agent Trajectory Prediction (TATP). Each clip is further annotated with an MTW-specific challenge taxonomy comprising dynamic ego-motion, weak traffic structure and contextual occlusion, enabling challenge-aware evaluation. We benchmark established conventional prediction models, general-purpose Vision-Language Models (VLMs), driving-specific VLMs and vision-language-action models. Our experiments reveal three key insights: (i) video backbones reach most of their full-observation accuracy from the first fifth of a maneuver, whereas zero-shot VLMs need most of the maneuver to be observed; (ii) zero-shot VLMs, whether general-purpose or driving-specific, largely remain close to simple baselines on both tasks; a preliminary LoRA study shows that adaptation lifts anticipation sharply but leaves trajectory prediction behind conventional models; and (iii) the rider's own motion drives forecasting difficulty: for every model, including a static baseline, errors are highest during left turns and rise under dynamic ego-motion. We believe MotoVerse will serve as a challenging benchmark for safer and more robust predictive AI for intelligent two-wheelers. The dataset and evaluation code are publicly available at https://github.com/VarunIIITH/MotoVerse.

paper_title: Intra-Architecture Source Attribution for Stable Diffusion: A New Task with Benchmark Dataset and Baseline
paper_abstract: Designing systems that attribute a generated image to its source model has lately become a major area of AI research. Most existing datasets and systems related to image source attribution are targeted towards the detection of architectural signatures of the source models. Distinct from this, focusing on stable diffusion, we introduce a novel task, IntrAA-SD, Intra-Architecture source Attribution for Stable Diffusion, where the source models to be differentiated share the same architectural backbone and differ only due to fine-tuning. The proposed task aligns with the emergence of fine-tuned generators having the same architecture, like Juggernaut XL and RealVis XL, which are fine-tuned versions of Stable Diffusion XL (SDXL). We provide a first-of-its-kind $140$K-image benchmark dataset containing images generated from different fine-tunes of SDXL, along with in-domain and out-of-distribution prompts. We also provide a baseline framework for IntrAA-SD, which leverages a style-conditioned Mixture-of-Experts network. It uses a frozen CLIP backbone to capture the image style and gate the MoE, which processes fine-tuned trace features from a high-resolution LoRA-adapted DINOv2 network. The fine-tuned models used, the prompting strategies considered, and the formation details employed in the novel dataset are elaborated. Our baseline intra-architecture source attribution method is evaluated in terms of attribution accuracy on our dataset, and ablation studies are also performed. Code and dataset is available at https://github.com/mallikagarg/IntrAA-SD.
comments: Accepted at IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision(WACV 2027)

paper_title: WayPOP: A Panoramic Open-Set Panoptic Tracking Benchmark
paper_abstract: Holistic perception for autonomous agents requires reliably segmenting and associating scene elements across time and camera views, including objects outside a fixed semantic taxonomy. Existing open-set panoptic benchmarks focus on individual images or views, while panoramic tracking benchmarks assume closed-set taxonomies. Consequently, these benchmarks do not evaluate whether unknown objects can be consistently segmented and tracked across synchronized multi-camera sequences. We introduce WayPOP, a panoramic open-set panoptic tracking benchmark built on real Waymo PVPS sequences augmented with diverse out-of-taxonomy 3D assets from Objaverse. Inserted objects are placed at fixed locations in the 3D scene and rendered using calibrated vehicle-mounted cameras as the ego vehicle and surrounding traffic move, providing temporally and cross-view consistent panoptic annotations and auxiliary LiDAR range observations. WayPOP contains approximately 670 curated assets instantiated as 980 unique unknown-object tracks, yielding 53,452 unknown-object mask annotations across 21,300 camera images. Our evaluation protocol defines a hierarchy of tasks from view-independent open-set panoptic segmentation to full panoramic open-set panoptic tracking, using known/unknown PQ and (w)STQ metrics. We benchmark representative open-set and open-vocabulary segmentation methods with temporal and cross-camera association. Our results reveal substantial limitations of current methods in truly open-set scenarios, highlighting robust unknown-object localization and identity association across time and views as major open challenges.

paper_title: SeVerus: Context-Aware, Gamified Benchmarking for Rust Verification
paper_abstract: Coding agents achieve high success rates on existing benchmarks for Verus, a verifier for Rust programs. These benchmarks typically provide the auxiliary lemmas needed to complete a proof. In practice, however, such lemmas must be discovered and proved. To capture this challenge, we present SEVERUS, a context-aware technique to generate Verus benchmarks that organizes verification tasks into quests, each divided into levelsin a gamified manner. Using the original proof dependencies in verified projects, SEVERUS constructs one quest per verification target and progressively removes proof context to create individual levels. These levels range from the easiest, requiring completing only a single missing lemma, to the hardest, requiring proving the target without any supporting lemmas. An independent checker rejects changes to executable code, weakened specifications, and unsound proof constructs. A noisy binary search estimates the highest level that an agent can solve reliably. Applied to six open-source Verus projects, SEVERUS generates 819 quests comprising 10,095 levels. Experiments with Codex using GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, and with Claude Code using Sonnet 4.6, show that success decreases and cost increases as proof context is withdrawn. The strongest agent solves the final level of 52 of 60 sampled quests, yet can only reliably solve 35% of their levels, with failures concentrated in longer quests. Successful GPT-6 Sol proofs rarely reproduce the withheld lemmas, instead, using alternative proof decompositions. By systematically varying proof context, SEVERUS provides a foundation for constructing verification benchmarks that can continue to challenge increasingly capable coding agents.

paper_title: Arctic-SAR: A Cross-Sensor RADARSAT Constellation Mission and Sentinel-1 Dataset and Fusion Benchmark for Multi-Task Sea Ice Mapping
paper_abstract: Current sea ice mapping benchmarks are mostly built around single-sensor SAR products, limiting the evaluation of cross-sensor variability and the effectiveness of combining observations from different SAR platforms. Models trained on such datasets may also be sensitive to sensor-specific artifacts, radiometric characteristics, and acquisition conditions, which can reduce robustness and limit generalization. To address these limitations, this study introduces Arctic-SAR, a cross-sensor SAR dataset for Arctic sea ice mapping, constructed by matching RADARSAT Constellation Mission (RCM) dual-polarization imagery with Sentinel-1 scenes from the AI4Arctic Sea Ice Dataset. The dataset consists of 221 co-registered scenes and supports multi-task prediction of sea ice concentration (SIC), stage of development (SOD), and floe size (FLOE). In addition to the dataset, we establish a benchmark for cross-sensor SAR sea ice mapping by quantifying the contribution of RCM imagery and evaluating single-sensor baselines alongside representative input-, feature-, and decision-level fusion strategies within a consistent multi-task U-Net framework. Across three independent runs, the test results show that the effectiveness of cross-sensor fusion is strongly dependent on the fusion strategy and prediction task. Decision-level fusion achieves the highest mean combined score of $77.28\pm0.29\%$, essentially matching the Sentinel-1-only baseline at $77.26\pm0.13\%$, while achieving the highest SIC \(R^2\) score. These findings show that Sentinel-1 and RCM provide task- and class-dependent information, but that simple joint cross-sensor fusion does not consistently improve generalization over a strong single-sensor baseline. Arctic-SAR therefore provides a benchmark for cross-sensor SAR fusion research in automated Arctic sea ice mapping.

paper_title: AgenticFinBench: Benchmarking Financial Agents on Diverse Tasks from Real-World Requests
paper_abstract: Financial agents are becoming an important class of real-world AI systems. Financial tasks vary widely in type and difficulty, and many are open-ended with no ground-truth answers. However, existing benchmarks neither capture this breadth and open-endedness nor separate grounding from correctness. To bridge this gap, we introduce $\textbf{AgenticFinBench}$, a benchmark of 230 real-world financial tasks spanning 8 categories, 2 languages, and 4 complexity levels. We also propose a reference-free evaluation framework that combines question-specific rubrics with a two-stage claim audit that detects hallucinations, defined as claims absent from the agent's trace and refuted by external evidence. This framework better matches how financial work is assessed in practice. Experiments across 18 agent configurations reveal three key findings: (1) Ignoring hallucinations can overstate agent performance: hallucination auditing lowers the baseline leader's score by 7.58 points and moves it to fourth place. (2) Harness differences explain more variation in evidence grounding than model differences (28.6% vs 8.8%). (3) Quality scores fall from 89.44 on direct retrieval to 79.18 on the most complex tasks. Case studies show that agents struggle to explain how events affect company profits or stock prices, compare financial data on a consistent basis, and justify their conclusions. By releasing AgenticFinBench, we aim to advance financial reasoning, factual verification, and agent design for more reliable responses to diverse real-world financial requests.

paper_title: <span data-teams="true">Data Descriptor: Dataset of Yeast Bioreactor Cultivation Dynamics with Integrated Inline and Offline Measurements
paper_abstract: We present a comprehensive, time-resolved dataset of yeast cultivation dynamics to support data-driven bioprocess engineering and process analytical technology development. The dataset comprises 52 controlled bioreactor cultivations of two industrially relevant yeast species, Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Saccharomyces pastorianus, each conducted over 72 – 76 h at two scales (0.7 L and 10 L working volume) under systematic parameter variation. A total of 43 variables are provided, comprising 30 inline variables (30 s resolution) and 13 offline variables sampled up to three times per day, enabling multimodal characterization of cultivation dynamics. Importantly, the dataset preserves real experimental conditions, including measurement noise, outliers, and different types of missing data arising from sensor failures, transmission errors, and process interruptions. By retaining these non-ideal characteristics, the dataset enables realistic evaluation of modeling, monitoring, and control approaches. It provides a valuable resource for dynamic process analysis, system identification, soft sensor development, fault detection, and validation of advanced data-driven methods under practical operating conditions.
comments: Preprints.org

paper_title: State-Level Validation of Syphilis and Chlamydia Transmission Models in the United States: An Open Surveillance Panel (2000–2024) and a Held-Out-Year Benchmark
paper_abstract: Transmission models of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are usually calibrated to national surveillance and are rarely tested against the case history of the individual states that run prevention programs. We assembled an open, documented panel of reported chlamydia and syphilis (primary and secondary, early non-primary non-secondary, unknown duration or late, and congenital) for the 50 U.S. states and the District of Columbia, 2000–2023, and for the nation, 2000–2024, by sex and age group, joined to a single consistent series of Census Bureau population estimates (262,958 rows). The panel reproduces the national totals exactly, and 21 of 22 named values match CDC’s published tables. We then calibrated two published compartmental models, a syphilis model with reinfection, two-stage treatment and treatment failure, and a chlamydia model with behavioral heterogeneity, to each jurisdiction’s 2011–2020 cases. We scored every fit on 2021–2023, years it never saw. With its published fixed settings, and the behavior-response strength scaled per capita to each state, the syphilis model had a median held-out mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 41.3%. It under-predicted in 44 of 51 jurisdictions (median bias-40.6%), because its prevalence-dependent behavior term capped incidence growth. Estimating the behavior-response strength reduced the median error to 17.6% (bias-1.2%; Wilcoxon p = 7.7 × 10−6). The fitted state values clustered around the published absolute value, not the per-capita one. The chlamydia model had a median held-out MAPE of 20.6% with a one-year infectious period, and 10.1% with the one-week period implied by treatment alone. In every fit, several parameters were not identifiable from annual counts. The panel, parameter sets with uncertainty ranges, validation scorecard, code, and an assumption register are openly released (DOIs 10.5281/zenodo.23742262 and 10.5281/zenodo.23742264).
comments: Preprints.org

paper_title: Visibility-Aware Reference Generation for Benchmarking Visual 3D Reconstruction in Vegetation-Rich Environments
paper_abstract: Reliable evaluation of visual 3D reconstruction and depth estimation in vegetation-rich outdoor environments is limited by the scarcity of geometric ground-truth data and the cost of complete scanner surveys. We present a LiDARbased reference-generation pipeline for evaluating the zero-shot performance of feed-forward visual-geometry models alongside conventional structure-from-motion (SfM) methods. The pipeline reuses camera images, LiDAR scans, and reference poses from existing multi-sensor localization datasets to generate per-view depth maps and visible reference point clouds. To address visibility errors in accumulated LiDAR scans, we introduce the LargeDepth-Gap Visibility Score (LDGVS) for point-wise visibility filtering and automatic scale selection in Hidden Point Removal(HPR). Experiments on TartanAirV2 and TartanGround show that, compared with Poisson surface reconstruction, which is an approach suited to completed scan surveys, the combined HPR and LDGVS filtering retains approximately three times the point density at comparable absolute relative error. We also apply the pipeline to the BotanicGarden dataset to systematically compare depth estimation and 3D reconstruction methods. Feedforward methods produce dense depth predictions efficiently, but their 3D reconstructions can contain duplicated structures. Conventional SfM generally produces more coherent geometry, but its reconstructions remain sparse and more prone to failure in challenging vegetated scenes. The benchmark toolkit and datasets will be released.
comments: 20 pages, 12 figures

paper_title: MedPhysBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Language Models on Medical Physics Calculations and Error Detection
paper_abstract: Medical physicists turn a prescription into a delivered dose and check one another's calculations, because one error in a beam calibration or a monitor-unit (MU) calculation can affect every patient treated with it. MedPhysBench has ten seeded generators of calculation items in radiation therapy, diagnostic imaging, nuclear medicine and radiation protection, up to clinical tasks such as a TG-51 calibration worksheet.
